title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 165 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 798–800 (Night 165, continuing directly from nights-164), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 165 continues the tale of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. The jeweller calms ʿAlī's household until ʿAlī comes round from his swoon and has him let go; he staggers home between two men, sleeps until mid-morning, and learns that some of his stolen goods have been thrown back at his door. Shaken, he repents of his part in the affair and keeps away from ʿAlī's house. Some time later he sees Shams al-Nahār's slave-girl in the street and hurries off in fear, but she follows him into an empty mosque, makes him swear to hear her out, and tells her story: when the men broke into his house, she and her mistress fled over the roofs, reached the Caliph's palace in a wretched state and hid what had happened; that night she had the boatman row her out to search the river for Shams al-Nahār, and at midnight a skiff came in with her mistress lying in it. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ وَالسِّتُّونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-khāmisatu wa-al-sittūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fifth-and-sixty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and sixty-fifth night,
sentences.n: The heading is built as before: al-khāmisa, “the fifth”, feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-sittūn, “and the sixty”; then baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْجَوْهَرِيَّ قَالَ لَهُمْ يَاقَوْمُ اسْمَعُوا كَلَامِي وَلَا تَفْعَلُوا بِي مَكْرُوهًا وَاصْبِرُوا وَهُوَ يُفِيقُ وَيُخْبِرُكُمْ بِقِصَّتِهِ بِنَفْسِهِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-jawhariyya qāla lahum yā qawmu ismaʿū kalāmī wa-lā tafʿalū bī makrūhan wa-iṣbirū wa-huwa yufīqu wa-yukhbirukum bi-qiṣṣatihi bi-nafsihi
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the jeweller said to-them: O people, hear my-speech, and do not do to-me a-hateful-thing; and be-patient, and he will-come-to and tell-you his-story by-himself.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the jeweller said to them, “Good people, hear what I have to say, and do me no harm. Be patient: he will come round and tell you his story himself.”
sentences.n: The print has السيعدان, a misprint for السعيدان, corrected here. The print also runs al-saʿīdu and anna together as one word, and that spacing is kept. The night picks up the jeweller's words where the last one broke off, repeating yā qawmu ismaʿū kalāmī; the print runs yā and qawmu together (ياقوم). faʿala bi-, “to do (something) to someone”: the person done to takes bi-; makrūh, “a hateful thing”, harm. wa-huwa yufīqu: the clause with wa- and a pronoun states what will follow if they wait, “and he will come to”; afāqa is to recover from a swoon. bi-nafsihi, “himself”, in his own person.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ شَدَّدْتُ عَلَيْهِمْ وَخَوَّفْتُهُمْ مِنَ الْفَضِيحَةِ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَهُمْ
sentences.tr: thumma shaddadtu ʿalayhim wa-khawwaftuhum mina al-faḍīḥati baynī wa-baynahum
sentences.l: Then I-was-firm upon-them and I-made-them-fear (from) the scandal between-me and between-them.
sentences.i: Then I was firm with them, and made them afraid of the scandal it would be for them and for me alike.
sentences.n: Back in the jeweller's own narration. shaddada ʿalā, “to be hard on, press”; khawwafa min, “to make (someone) fear (something)”: min marks the thing feared. al-faḍīḥa baynī wa-baynahum, “the scandal between me and them”: a disgrace that would touch both sides, since the affair concerns the Caliph's favourite.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا نَحْنُ كَذَلِكَ وَإِذَا بِعَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ تَحَرَّكَ فِي فِرَاشِهِ فَفَرِحَ أَهْلُهُ وَانْصَرَفَ النَّاسُ عَنْهُ وَمَنَعَنِي أَهْلُهُ مِنَ الْخُرُوجِ مِنْ عِنْدِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā naḥnu kadhālika wa-idhā bi-ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin taḥarraka fī firāshihi fa-fariḥa ahluhu wa-inṣarafa al-nāsu ʿanhu wa-manaʿanī ahluhu mina al-khurūji min ʿindihi
sentences.l: And while we (were) thus, and behold, ʿAlī ibn Bakkār moved in his-bed; and his-family rejoiced, and the people went-away from-him, and his-family prevented-me from the going-out from with-him.
sentences.i: And while we were so, all at once ʿAlī ibn Bakkār stirred in his bed. His household rejoiced, the people left him, and his family would not let me leave his side.
sentences.n: baynamā … wa-idhā, “while … behold”: the usual frame for a sudden turn. After idhā of surprise, bi- only marks what appears, here ʿAlī himself. manaʿa min, “to prevent from”: what is prevented takes min; min ʿindihi, “from his presence”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَشُّوا مَاءَ الْوَرْدِ عَلَى وَجْهِهِ فَلَمَّا أَفَاقَ وَشَمَّ الْهَوَاءَ صَارُوا يَسْأَلُونَهُ عَنْ حَالِهِ فَصَارَ يُخْبِرُهُمْ وَلِسَانُهُ لَايَرُدُّ جَوَابًا بِسُرْعَةٍ
sentences.tr: thumma rashshū māʾa al-wardi ʿalā wajhihi fa-lammā afāqa wa-shamma al-hawāʾa ṣārū yasʾalūnahu ʿan ḥālihi fa-ṣāra yukhbiruhum wa-lisānuhu lā yaruddu jawāban bi-surʿatin
sentences.l: Then they-sprinkled the water of the rose upon his-face; and when he-came-to and smelt the air, they-began asking-him about his-state; and he-began telling-them, and his-tongue (was) not returning an-answer with-speed.
sentences.i: Then they sprinkled rosewater on his face, and when he came to himself and breathed the air, they began to ask him how he was. He set about telling them, but his tongue was slow to give an answer.
sentences.n: māʾ al-ward, “rose-water”, the usual restorative for a swoon. shamma al-hawāʾ, “he smelt the air”, he drew breath again. ṣāra with an imperfect, “began to (do)”, a Middle Arabic favourite, twice here. The print runs lā and yaruddu together (لايرد); the shaddas of رشّوا and شمّ are the print's own. radda jawāban, “to return an answer”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَشَارَ إِلَيْهِمْ أَنْ يُطْلِقُونِي لِأَذْهَبَ إِلَى مَنْزِلِي فَأَطْلَقُونِي
sentences.tr: thumma ashāra ilayhim an yuṭliqūnī li-adhhaba ilā manzilī fa-aṭlaqūnī
sentences.l: Then he-signed to-them that they-release-me so-that-I-go to my-dwelling; and they-released-me.
sentences.i: Then he signed to them to let me go, so that I could go home; and they let me go.
sentences.n: ashāra ilā … an, “to sign to (someone) that he should”: the thing signalled follows as an an-clause. yuṭliqūnī is subjunctive after an (the plural's -na dropped). li-adhhaba, “so that I may go”: li- of purpose with the subjunctive.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجْتُ وَأَنَا لَا أُصَدِّقُ بِالْخَلَاصِ وَأَتَيْتُ إِلَى دَارِي وَأَنَا بَيْنَ رَجُلَيْنِ حَتَّى وَصَلْتُ إِلَى أَهْلِي
sentences.tr: fa-kharajtu wa-anā lā uṣaddiqu bi-al-khalāṣi wa-ataytu ilā dārī wa-anā bayna rajulayni ḥattā waṣaltu ilā ahlī
sentences.l: And I-went-out, and I (was) not believing in the deliverance; and I-came to my-house, and I (was) between two-men, until I-reached my-family.
sentences.i: So I went out, scarcely able to believe I was free, and made my way home held up between two men until I reached my family.
sentences.n: wa-anā …, “while I …”: a circumstantial clause, twice here. ṣaddaqa bi-, “to believe in”: the verb takes bi- for the thing believed. bayna rajulayni, “between two men”: supported on either side, too weak to walk alone. ahlī, “my family”, the household at home.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَوْنِي عَلَى تِلْكَ الْحَالَةِ قَامُوا بِالْعِيَاطِ وَلَطَمُوا عَلَى وُجُوهِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾawnī ʿalā tilka al-ḥālati qāmū bi-al-ʿiyāṭi wa-laṭamū ʿalā wujūhihim
sentences.l: And when they-saw-me in that state, they-rose with the wailing and they-slapped on their-faces.
sentences.i: When they saw me in that state they raised a wailing and beat their faces.
sentences.n: ʿiyāṭ, “wailing, crying out”, is a colloquial word (Classical ṣiyāḥ); qāma bi-, “to set about, start up”, with bi- for the thing begun: “they broke into wailing”. laṭama ʿalā wajhihi, to slap one's face in grief, the women's gesture of mourning.

sentences.t: فَأَوْمَأْتُ إِلَيْهِمْ بِيَدِي أَنِ اسْكُتُوا فَسَكَتُوا
sentences.tr: fa-awmaʾtu ilayhim bi-yadī ani uskutū fa-sakatū
sentences.l: And I-signed to-them with-my-hand that be-silent; and they-were-silent.
sentences.i: I signed to them with my hand to be quiet, and they were quiet.
sentences.n: awmaʾa ilā, “to make a sign to”; bi-yadī, “with my hand”, bi- of the instrument. an before an imperative gives the content of the sign, “that is: be silent”; its kasra joins it to uskutū.

sentences.t: وَانْصَرَفَ الرَّجُلَانِ إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِهِمَا وَانْقَلَبْتُ عَلَى فِرَاشِي بَقِيَّةَ لَيْلَتِي وَلَمْ أُفِقْ إِلَّا وَقْتَ الضُّحَى
sentences.tr: wa-inṣarafa al-rajulāni ilā ḥāli sabīlihimā wa-inqalabtu ʿalā firāshī baqiyyata laylatī wa-lam ufiq illā waqta al-ḍuḥā
sentences.l: And the two-men went-off to the state of their-way, and I-turned-over on my-bed the rest of my-night, and I did-not come-to except (at) the time of the forenoon.
sentences.i: The two men went their way, and I lay tossing on my bed for the rest of the night, and did not come to myself until the middle of the morning.
sentences.n: ilā ḥāli sabīlihimā, “to the state of their way”: a fixed phrase, “about their business”. inqalaba, “to turn over”, here to lie tossing. lam … illā, “not … except”, “not until”. al-ḍuḥā, the forenoon, when the sun is well up. The shadda of الّا is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدْتُ أَهْلِي مُجْتَمِعِينَ حَوْلِي فَقَالُوا مَا الَّذِي دَهَاكَ وَبِشَرِّهِ رَمَاكَ
sentences.tr: fa-wajadtu ahlī mujtamiʿīna ḥawlī fa-qālū mā alladhī dahāka wa-bi-sharrihi ramāka
sentences.l: And I-found my-family gathered around-me, and they-said: What (is) that-which befell-you, (dahāka) and with-its-evil struck-you (ramāka)?
sentences.i: I found my family gathered round me, and they said, “What is it that has befallen you, and struck you down with its evil?”
sentences.n: The question rhymes, dahāka / ramāka, a small piece of sajʿ. dahā, “to befall (as a calamity)”; ramā bi-, “to strike with”, bi- of the instrument: the thing that befell him is pictured as hurling its evil at him.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ ائْتُونِي بِشَيْءٍ مِنَ الشَّرَابِ فَجَٰأُوا لِي شَرَابًا فَشَرِبْتُ مِنْهُ حَتَّى اسْتَكْفَيْتُ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu iʾtūnī bi-shayʾin mina al-sharābi fa-jāʾū lī sharāban fa-sharibtu minhu ḥattā istakfaytu
sentences.l: And I-said: Bring-me some-thing of the drink. And they-came to-me (with) a-drink, and I-drank of-it until I-had-enough.
sentences.i: I said, “Bring me something to drink.” They brought me a drink, and I drank until I had had enough.
sentences.n: atā bi-, “to bring”: the verb takes bi- for the thing brought (iʾtūnī bi-shayʾin, “bring me something”). jāʾū is printed فجأوا: the hamza is set on the alif and the long ā has no letter of its own, so it is supplied with a dagger alif. jāʾa lī sharāban, “they came to me a drink”, leaves out the bi- that the Classical “brought” needs (jāʾū bi-sharābin): the colloquial sense “bring” for jāʾa, taking a direct object. sharāb, “drink”, may be wine or any drink. istakfā, “to have one's fill”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قُلْتُ لَهُمْ قَدْ كَانَ مَاكَانَ فَانْصَرَفُوا إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِهِمْ
sentences.tr: thumma qultu lahum qad kāna mā kāna fa-inṣarafū ilā ḥāli sabīlihim
sentences.l: Then I-said to-them: What was has-been. And they-went-off to the state of their-way.
sentences.i: Then I said to them, “What is done is done,” and they went about their business.
sentences.n: qad kāna mā kāna, “there was what there was”: a set phrase closing a subject without explaining it. The print runs mā and kāna together (ماكان).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اعْتَذَرْتُ إِلَى أَصْحَابِي وَسَأَلْتُهُمْ عَنِ الَّذِي ذَهَبَ مِنْ دَارِي هَلْ عَادَ شَيْءٌ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: thumma iʿtadhartu ilā aṣḥābī wa-saʾaltuhum ʿani alladhī dhahaba min dārī hal ʿāda shayʾun minhu
sentences.l: Then I-made-excuse to my-companions, and I-asked-them about that-which went from my-house: had anything of-it returned?
sentences.i: Then I made my excuses to my friends and asked them whether any of what had been taken from my house had come back.
sentences.n: iʿtadhara ilā, “to apologise to”: the person addressed takes ilā. His friends are those whose borrowed things were lost in the raid. alladhī dhahaba min dārī, “what went from my house”, the goods stolen in the raid, which the thieves had undertaken to return.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا عَادَ الْبَعْضُ وَسَبَبُهُ أَنَّهُ جَاءَ إِنْسَانٌ وَرَمَاهُ فِي بَابِ الدَّارِ وَلَمْ نَنْظُرْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū ʿāda al-baʿḍu wa-sababuhu annahu jāʾa insānun wa-ramāhu fī bābi al-dāri wa-lam nanẓurhu
sentences.l: And they-said: The part has-returned; and its-cause (is) that-it (was that) a-person came and threw-it in the door of the house, and we did-not see-him.
sentences.i: They said, “Some of it has come back. A man came and threw it down at the door of the house, and we did not see him.”
sentences.n: al-baʿḍ, “the part”, “some of it”. annahu jāʾa, “that (it was that) … came”: the -hu is the pronoun of the matter, pointing to the clause that follows, not to a person. naẓara with a direct object, “to see”, is colloquial; Classical prefers naẓara ilā, “to look at”, or raʾā.

sentences.t: فَسَلَّيْتُ نَفْسِى وَأَقَمْتُ فِي مَكَانِي يَوْمَيْنِ وَأَنَا لَاأَقْدِرُ عَلَى الْقِيَامِ مِنْ مَحَلِّي
sentences.tr: fa-sallaytu nafsī wa-aqamtu fī makānī yawmayni wa-anā lā aqdiru ʿalā al-qiyāmi min maḥallī
sentences.l: And I-consoled myself, and I-stayed in my-place two-days, and I (was) not able for the rising from my-place.
sentences.i: So I consoled myself, and stayed where I was for two days, unable to get up from my bed.
sentences.n: sallā nafsahu, “to console oneself”. qadara ʿalā, “to be able to”: the verb takes ʿalā for the thing one can do. The print runs lā and aqdiru together (لااقدر), spells nafsī with ى, and gives the shadda of محلّي; maḥall, “place, spot”, here the place he lay.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَوَّيْتُ نَفْسِي وَمَشَيْتُ حَتَّى دَخَلْتُ الْحَمَّامَ وَأَنَا عِنْدِى تَعَبٌ شَدِيدٌ وَقَلْبِي مَشْغُولٌ مِنْ جِهَةِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَشَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: thumma qawwaytu nafsī wa-mashaytu ḥattā dakhaltu al-ḥammāma wa-anā ʿindī taʿabun shadīdun wa-qalbī mashghūlun min jihati ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-Shamsi al-Nahāri
sentences.l: Then I-strengthened myself and I-walked until I-entered the bath-house, and I — with-me (was) severe weariness, and my-heart (was) busied from the direction of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār.
sentences.i: Then I took heart and walked as far as the bath-house and went in, though I was sorely weary, and my heart was full of care for ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār.
sentences.n: qawwā nafsahu, “to strengthen oneself”, to rally. ʿindī taʿabun, “with me is weariness”, “I have”: the usual Arabic way of saying “have”. mashghūl min jihati, “busied on account of”, anxious about; min jihati, “from the side of, concerning”. The print spells ʿindī with ى and gives the shadda of قوّيت.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ أَسْمَعْ لَهُمَا خَبَرًا فِي تِلْكَ الْمُدَّةِ وَلَمْ أَسْتَطِعِ الْوُصُولَ إِلَى دَارِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَلَمْ يَسْتَقِرَّلِي قَرَارٌ فِي مَكَانِي خَوْفًا عَلَى نَفْسِي
sentences.tr: wa-lam asmaʿ lahumā khabaran fī tilka al-muddati wa-lam astaṭiʿi al-wuṣūla ilā dāri ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-lam yastaqirra lī qarārun fī makānī khawfan ʿalā nafsī
sentences.l: And I did-not hear of-them-two a-tiding in that period, and I was-not-able the reaching to the house of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and there did-not settle for-me a-settling in my-place, (for) fear for myself.
sentences.i: In all that time I heard no news of the two of them; I could not bring myself to go to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār's house, and I could not rest easy in my own place for fear for my life.
sentences.n: lahumā, “of the two”: li- here marks whom the news concerns. lam astaṭiʿi: the jussive's final sukūn takes a kasra before the article. lam yastaqirra lī qarārun, “no settling settled for me”, “I could find no rest”: verb and subject from the same root. The print runs yastaqirra and lī together (يستقرلي). khawfan ʿalā, “fearing for”, an accusative of reason.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تُبْتُ إِلَى اللَّهِ تَعَالَى مِمَّا صَدَرَ مِنِّي وَحَمِدْتُهُ عَلَى سَلَامَتِي
sentences.tr: thumma tubtu ilā Allāhi taʿālā mimmā ṣadara minnī wa-ḥamidtuhu ʿalā salāmatī
sentences.l: Then I-repented to God — exalted (is He) — of-what had-issued from-me, and I-praised-Him for my-safety.
sentences.i: Then I turned in repentance to God Most High for what I had done, and praised Him that I was safe.
sentences.n: tāba ilā Allāh min, “to turn in repentance to God from”: God takes ilā, the sin min. mā ṣadara minnī, “what issued from me”: his part in the lovers' secret dealings behind the Caliph's back. ḥamida ʿalā, “to praise (God) for”.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ مُدَّةٍ حَدَّثَتْنِي نَفْسِي أَنْ أَتَّصِلَ تِلْكَ النَّاحِيَةَ وَأَرْجِعَ فِي سَاعَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda muddatin ḥaddathatnī nafsī an attaṣila tilka al-nāḥiyata wa-arjiʿa fī sāʿatin
sentences.l: And after a-while my-soul spoke-to-me that I-reach that quarter and return in an-hour.
sentences.i: After a while my heart told me to go over to that quarter and be back within the hour.
sentences.n: ḥaddathathu nafsuhu an, “his soul told him to”, he had a mind to. ittaṣala, “to reach”, with a direct object, is loose; Classical says ittaṣala bi- or ilā. tilka al-nāḥiya, “that quarter”, presumably the neighbourhood of ʿAlī's house. fī sāʿatin, “in an hour”, quickly.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَرَدْتُ الْمَسِيرَ رَأَيْتُ امْرَأَةً وَاقِفَةً فَتَأَمَّلْتُهَا وَإِذَاهِيَ جَارِيَةُ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aradtu al-masīra raʾaytu imraʾatan wāqifatan fa-taʾammaltuhā wa-idhā hiya jāriyatu Shamsi al-Nahāri
sentences.l: And when I-wanted the going, I-saw a-woman standing; and I-looked-closely-at-her, and behold, she (was) the slave-girl of Shams al-Nahār.
sentences.i: When I was about to set out, I saw a woman standing there. I looked at her closely, and it was Shams al-Nahār's slave-girl.
sentences.n: taʾammala, “to look at closely, scrutinise”. wa-idhā hiya, “and behold, she …”: idhā of surprise; the print runs idhā and hiya together (واذاهي). jāriya, “slave-girl”, the confidante who has carried messages between the lovers throughout.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا عَرَفْتُهَا سِرْتُ وَهَرْوَلْتُ فِي سَيْرِى فَتَبِعَتْنِي فَدَاخَلَنِي مِنْهَا الْفَزَعُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ʿaraftuhā sirtu wa-harwaltu fī sayrī fa-tabiʿatnī fa-dākhalanī minhā al-fazaʿu
sentences.l: And when I-knew-her, I-went-on and I-hurried in my-going; and she-followed-me, and there-entered-me from-her the fright.
sentences.i: When I knew her I walked on, quickening my pace, but she followed me, and I was seized with fright of her.
sentences.n: harwala, “to hurry, go at a jog-trot”, between walking and running. dākhala, “to enter into, pervade”, with the feeling as subject: “fear entered me”; minhā, “from her”, of her. The print spells sayrī with ى.

sentences.t: وَصِرْتُ كُلَّمَا أَنْظُرُهَا يَأْخُذُنِي الرُّعْبُ مِنْهَا وَهِيَ تَقُولُ لِي قِفْ حَتَّى أُحَدِّثَكَ بِشَيْءٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣirtu kullamā anẓuruhā yaʾkhudhunī al-ruʿbu minhā wa-hiya taqūlu lī qif ḥattā uḥaddithaka bi-shayʾin
sentences.l: And I-came-to-be, whenever I-see-her, the terror of-her takes-me, and she (was) saying to-me: Stop, so-that I-tell-you of-something.
sentences.i: Every time I looked at her, terror of her took hold of me, while she kept calling to me, “Stop, so that I can tell you something.”
sentences.n: ṣirtu, “I came to be”, sets up a repeated state. kullamā, “whenever”, takes the imperfect here (anẓuruhā), where Classical prefers the perfect: a Middle Arabic habit. naẓara again with a direct object, “to see, look at”. ḥattā with the subjunctive, “so that”. ḥaddatha bi-, “to tell (someone) of”, with bi- for the matter told.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا لَمْ أَلْتَفِتْ إِلَيْهَا وَلَمْ أَزَلْ سَائِرًا إِلَى مَسْجِدٍ فِى مَوْضِعٍ خَالٍ مِنَ النَّاسِ
sentences.tr: wa-anā lam altafit ilayhā wa-lam azal sāʾiran ilā masjidin fī mawḍiʿin khālin mina al-nāsi
sentences.l: And I did-not turn to-her, and I did-not cease going to a-mosque in a-place empty of the people.
sentences.i: But I did not turn to look at her, and kept walking until I came to a mosque in a spot where no one was about.
sentences.n: iltafata ilā, “to turn (the face) towards”. lam azal, “I did not cease”, with an accusative participle, “I kept going”. khālin, “empty”, the defective participle of khalā, with min for what the place is empty of. The print spells fī with ى.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لِي ادْخُلْ فِي هَذَا الْمَسْجِدِ لِأَ قُولَ لَكَ كَلِمَةً وَلَا تَخَفْ مِنْ شَيْءٍ وَحَلَّفَتْنِي
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lī udkhul fī hādhā al-masjidi li-aqūla laka kalimatan wa-lā takhaf min shayʾin wa-ḥallafatnī
sentences.l: And she-said to-me: Enter into this mosque so-that-I-say to-you a-word, and do-not fear (from) anything. And she-adjured-me.
sentences.i: She said to me, “Go into this mosque, so that I can say a word to you, and do not be afraid of anything,” and she pressed me with oaths.
sentences.n: The print sets لا قول as two words; it is read li-aqūla, “so that I may say”, li- of purpose with the subjunctive, the alif of aqūla split off with the lām, and not lā qawla, “no speech”. dakhala fī, “to go into”, with fī, beside the bare object in the next sentence. khāfa min, “to fear”: min marks the thing feared. ḥallafa, “to make (someone) swear, to adjure”: she begged him by oaths to do as she asked.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلْتُ الْمَسْجِدَ وَدَخَلَتْ خَلْفِي فَصَلَّيْتُ رَكْعَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhaltu al-masjida wa-dakhalat khalfī fa-ṣallaytu rakʿatayni
sentences.l: And I-entered the mosque, and she-entered behind-me, and I-prayed two-rakʿas.
sentences.i: So I went into the mosque, and she came in behind me, and I prayed two rakʿas.
sentences.n: rakʿa, a single cycle of the ritual prayer, with its bowing and prostrations; two rakʿas are the shortest voluntary prayer, the customary greeting of a mosque on entering. The shadda of صلّيت is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَقَدَّمْتُ إِلَيْهَا وَأَنَا أَتَأَوَّهُ وَقُلْتُ لَهَا مَا بَالُكِ فَسَأَلَتْنِي عَنْ حَالِي
sentences.tr: thumma taqaddamtu ilayhā wa-anā ataʾawwahu wa-qultu lahā mā bāluki fa-saʾalatnī ʿan ḥālī
sentences.l: Then I-went-forward to-her, and I (was) sighing, and I-said to-her: What (is) your-matter? And she-asked-me about my-state.
sentences.i: Then I went up to her, sighing, and said to her, “What is the matter with you?” And she asked me how I was.
sentences.n: taʾawwaha, “to say āh”, to sigh or groan; the shadda of اتأوّه and the damma of تقدمتُ are the print's own. mā bāluki, “what is your case?”, “what is the matter with you?”, with the feminine -ki for the girl.

sentences.t: فَحَدَّثْتُهَا بِمَا وَقَعَ لِي وَأَخْبَرْتُهَا بِمَا جَرَى لِعَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَقُلْتُ لَهَا مَا خَبَرُكِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥaddathtuhā bi-mā waqaʿa lī wa-akhbartuhā bi-mā jarā li-ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-qultu lahā mā khabaruki
sentences.l: And I-told-her of-what befell me, and I-informed-her of-what happened to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and I-said to-her: What (is) your-news?
sentences.i: So I told her what had befallen me, and what had happened to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and said to her, “And how is it with you?”
sentences.n: The jeweller answers her question first and then puts his own again. ḥaddatha bi- and akhbara bi-, “to tell (someone) of”: both verbs take the person told as object and the matter told with bi-. mā khabaruki, “what is your news?”, with the feminine -ki, is the stock way of asking how things stand with someone.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ اعْلَمْ أَنِّي لَمَّا رَأَيْتُ الرِّجَالَ كَسَرُوا بَابَ دَارِكَ وَدَخَلُوا خِفْتُ مِنْهُمْ وَخَشِيتُ أَنْ يَكُونُوا مِنْ عِنْدِ الْخَلِيفَةِ فَيَأْخُذُونَنِي أَنَا وَسَيِّدَتِي فَنَهْلِكُ فِي وَقْتِنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālati iʿlam annī lammā raʾaytu al-rijāla kasarū bāba dārika wa-dakhalū khiftu minhum wa-khashītu an yakūnū min ʿindi al-khalīfati fa-yaʾkhudhūnanī anā wa-sayyidatī fa-nahliku fī waqtinā
sentences.l: And she-said: Know that-I, when I-saw the men (that) they-broke the door of-your-house and they-entered, I-feared (from) them, and I-dreaded that they-be from the side of the Caliph, and they-take-me, I and my-lady, and we-perish in our-time.
sentences.i: She said, “Know that when I saw the men break down the door of your house and come in, I was afraid of them, and dreaded that they had come from the Caliph and would seize me and my lady, and we should perish on the spot.
sentences.n: The slave-girl now tells her own story in the first person, inside the jeweller's narration: her “I” is not his. annī … khiftu: the sentence opened by “know that I” is completed only after the lammā clause, by khiftu, “I feared”; the kasra of خِفت is the print's own. kasarū, “they broke”, stands loosely after raʾaytu, “I saw the men (who) broke”. min ʿindi al-khalīfa, “from the Caliph”, i.e. sent by him. fa-yaʾkhudhūnanī, “and they would seize me”: after an … fa- Classical Arabic wants the subjunctive (fa-yaʾkhudhūnī); the print keeps the indicative ending -ūna, a common Middle Arabic feature, and fa-nahliku, “and we should perish”, is read as indicative with it. anā wa-sayyidatī: the independent pronoun repeats the object -nī so that “my lady” can be joined to it. fī waqtinā, “in our very time”, “then and there”. The hamza of يأخذونني is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَهَرَبْتُ مِنَ السُّطُوحِ أَنَا وَالْوَصِيفَتَانِ وَرَمَيْنَا أَنْفُسَنَا مِنْ مَكَانٍ عَالٍ وَدَخَلْنَا عَلَى قَوْمٍ فَهَرَبْنَا عِنْدَهُمْ وَأَوْصَلُونَا إِلَى قَصْرِ الْخِلَافَةِ وَنَحْنُ عَلَى أَقْبَحِ صِفَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-harabtu mina al-suṭūḥi anā wa-al-waṣīfatāni wa-ramaynā anfusanā min makānin ʿālin wa-dakhalnā ʿalā qawmin fa-harabnā ʿindahum wa-awṣalūnā ilā qaṣri al-khilāfati wa-naḥnu ʿalā aqbaḥi ṣifatin
sentences.l: And I-fled from (by-way-of) the roofs, I and the two-maids, and we-threw ourselves from a-place high, and we-entered upon a-people, and we-fled with-them, and they-brought-us to the palace of the Caliphate, and we (were) upon the ugliest of states.
sentences.i: So I fled over the roofs, I and the two maids, and we threw ourselves down from a high place and came in upon some people, and took refuge with them; and they brought us to the Caliph's palace, in the sorriest plight.
sentences.n: anā wa-al-waṣīfatāni: the pronoun restates the subject of harabtu so that “the two maids” (nominative dual) can be joined to it; the verbs then go into the plural, ramaynā, “we threw”. waṣīfa, “maidservant”. dakhala ʿalā, “to come in upon (people)”. fa-harabnā ʿindahum, literally “we fled with them”: haraba ʿinda is unusual, and the sense seems to be that the fugitives took refuge in that household. qaṣr al-khilāfa, “the palace of the caliphate”, the Caliph's palace, where Shams al-Nahār lives. wa-naḥnu ʿalā aqbaḥi ṣifatin, “we being in the worst of conditions”, a circumstantial clause introduced by wa-.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخْفَيْنَا أَمْرَنَا وَصِرْنَا نَتَقَلَّبُ عَلَى الْجَمْرِ إِلَى أَنْ جَنَّ اللَّيْلُ
sentences.tr: thumma akhfaynā amranā wa-ṣirnā nataqallabu ʿalā al-jamri ilā an janna al-laylu
sentences.l: Then we-hid our-affair, and we-came-to-be turning-over on the coals, until (that) the night fell.
sentences.i: Then we kept the matter hidden, and lay tossing as if on live coals until night came down.
sentences.n: akhfaynā amranā, “we hid our affair”, told no one what had happened. ṣirnā nataqallabu ʿalā al-jamri, “we took to turning over on the embers”: ṣāra with an imperfect, “to begin, take to”; turning on hot coals is the image of restless anguish. ilā an, “until”. The shadda of جنّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَفَتَحْتُ بَابَ الْبَحْرِ وَاسْتَدْعَيْتُ بِالْمَلَّاحِ الَّذِي أَخْرَجَنَا تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ وَقُلْتُ لَهُ إِنَّ سَيِّدَتِي لَمْ نَعْلَمْ لَهَا خَبَرًا فَاحْمِلْنِي فِى الزَّوْرَقِ حَتَّى أَذْهَبُ وَأُفَتِّشُ عَلَيْهَا فِى الْبَحْرِ لَعَلِّي أَقَعُ عَلَى خَبَرِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-fataḥtu bāba al-baḥri wa-istadʿaytu bi-al-mallāḥi alladhī akhrajanā tilka al-laylata wa-qultu lahu inna sayyidatī lam naʿlam lahā khabaran fa-iḥmilnī fī al-zawraqi ḥattā adhhabu wa-ufattishu ʿalayhā fī al-baḥri laʿallī aqaʿu ʿalā khabarihā
sentences.l: And I-opened the gate of the river, and I-summoned (for) the boatman who took-us-out that night, and I-said to-him: (Indeed) my-lady, we-have-not-known of-her any news; so carry-me in the skiff, so-that I-go and I-search for-her on the river; perhaps-I fall upon news-of-her.
sentences.i: Then I opened the river gate and sent for the boatman who had taken us out that night, and said to him, ‘We have had no word of my lady; so take me in the skiff, that I may go and search for her on the river, in case I come upon some news of her.’
sentences.n: bāb al-baḥr, “the gate of the sea”, is the palace's water gate: al-baḥr here is the Tigris, as often in the Nights. istadʿā, “to summon, send for”, normally takes a direct object; here, like daʿā bi-, “call for”, it takes bi-. The boatman is the one who had taken the women out on the night of their visit to the jeweller's house. inna sayyidatī lam naʿlam lahā khabaran: “my lady” is set first as the topic and taken up again by lahā, “as for my lady, we know no news of her”. ḥattā adhhabu wa-ufattishu, “so that I may go and search”: the dammas on both verbs are the print's own, an indicative where Classical Arabic has the subjunctive after purposive ḥattā; the shadda of افتّش is also printed. fattasha ʿalā, “to search for”, is Middle Arabic for Classical fattasha ʿan. waqaʿa ʿalā, “to fall upon”, “come upon, light on”. The shadda of لعلّي is the print's own, and the print spells fī with ى.

sentences.t: فَحَمَلَنِي فِى الزَّوْرَقِ وَسَارَبِي وَلَمْ أَزَلْ سَائِرَةً فِى الْبَحْرِ حَتَّى انْتَصَفَ اللَّيْلُ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥamalanī fī al-zawraqi wa-sāra bī wa-lam azal sāʾiratan fī al-baḥri ḥattā intaṣafa al-laylu
sentences.l: And he-carried-me in the skiff and he-went with-me, and I-did-not cease going on the river until the night reached-its-middle.
sentences.i: He took me in the skiff and set off with me, and I went on and on along the river until it was midnight.
sentences.n: The print runs sāra and bī together (ساربي); it is kept as one word. sāra bī, “he went with me”, carried me along. lam azal sāʾiratan, “I did not cease going”, I kept going; sāʾira is feminine, as the speaker is a woman, and its hamza is printed. ḥattā with the perfect is simply “until”. intaṣafa al-laylu, “the night was halved”, midnight came.

sentences.t: فَرَأَيْتُ سُمَيْرِيَّةً أَقْبَلَتْ إِلَى جِهَةِ الْبَابِ وَفِيهَا رَجُلٌ يَقْذِفُ وَمَعَهُ رَجُلٌ آخَرُ وَاقِفٌ وَامْرَأَةٌ مَطْرُوحَةٌ بَيْنَهُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-raʾaytu sumayriyyatan aqbalat ilā jihati al-bābi wa-fīhā rajulun yaqdhifu wa-maʿahu rajulun ākharu wāqifun wa-imraʾatun maṭrūḥatun baynahumā
sentences.l: And I-saw a-sumayriyya (that) came-on toward the direction of the gate, and in-it a-man rowing, and with-him a-man other standing, and a-woman thrown-down between-the-two-of-them.
sentences.i: Then I saw a boat coming toward the gate, and in it a man rowing, and with him another man standing, and a woman lying stretched out between them.
sentences.n: sumayriyya is a kind of small river boat of Baghdad and the Tigris; its damma, fatḥa and shadda are the print's own. aqbalat …, “(which) was coming”, describes the indefinite noun with no relative word, as Arabic does after an indefinite. qadhafa, “to throw”, is used of a boatman for rowing, plying the oars. maṭrūḥa, “thrown down”, lying helpless. The madda of آخر and the hamza of امرأة are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَمَا زَالَ يَقْذِفُ إِلَى أَنْ وَصَلَتْ إِلَى الْبَرِّ
sentences.tr: wa-mā zāla yaqdhifu ilā an waṣalat ilā al-barri
sentences.l: And he-did-not cease rowing until (that) it-reached to the land.
sentences.i: He went on rowing until the boat came to land.
sentences.n: mā zāla with an imperfect, “he did not cease (doing)”, he kept on. waṣalat, “it (f.) reached”, is read of the boat, sumayriyya being feminine; waṣaltu, “I reached”, is also possible from the letters, but it is the boat that is coming in. al-barr, “dry land”, the bank.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَزَلَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ تَأَمَّلْتُهَا فَإِذَا هِيَ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā nazalati al-marʾatu taʾammaltuhā fa-idhā hiya Shamsu al-Nahāri
sentences.l: And when the woman got-out, I-looked-closely-at-her, and behold, she (was) Shams al-Nahār.
sentences.i: When the woman came ashore I looked hard at her, and behold, it was Shams al-Nahār.
sentences.n: nazala, “to come down”, is used of leaving a boat (or a mount): she got out on to the bank. taʾammala, “to look at closely, scrutinise”; its hamza, like that of المرأة, is the print's. fa-idhā hiya, “and behold, she was”, the idhā of sudden discovery.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلْتُ إِلَيْهَا وَقَدِ انْدَهَشْتُ مِنَ الْفَرْحَةِ لَمَّا رَأَيْتُهَا بَعْدَ مَا قَطَعْتُ الرَّجَاءَ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-nazaltu ilayhā wa-qadi indahashtu mina al-farḥati lammā raʾaytuhā baʿda mā qaṭaʿtu al-rajāʾa minhā
sentences.l: And I-went-down to-her, and (already) I-was-dazed from the joy, when I-saw-her, after (that) I-had-cut-off the hope of-her.
sentences.i: So I went down to her, beside myself for joy at seeing her, when I had given up all hope of her.
sentences.n: nazaltu ilayhā, “I went down to her”, from the skiff or the gate to where she lay. wa-qad indahashtu, “I having been dazed”, a circumstantial clause with qad. indahasha, Form VII of dahisha, “to be bewildered, beside oneself”, is a post-Classical form. al-farḥa, “joy”, a feminine beside the commoner faraḥ. qaṭaʿa al-rajāʾa min, “to cut off hope of”, to despair of; baʿda mā, “after”. The hamza of رأيتها is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she-fell-silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The object comes before the subject: Shahrazāda is the one overtaken, al-ṣabāḥu the morning that overtakes. The print sets the name as one word here (شهرزاد). al-kalām al-mubāḥ, “the permitted speech”, the talk allowed her until dawn; the rhyme ṣabāḥ / mubāḥ closes every night.
